title: Nonliving Things Help Decide Who Lives Where

scenes.tts: The James River starts as fresh water in Virginia's mountains. It ends in the salty Chesapeake Bay. Wild oyster reefs grow in the lower river. Near Richmond, the water is fresh, and oysters can die. So why do different living things live in a mountain stream, a forest, and the salty Bay?

scenes.tts: Every place has an ecosystem. An ecosystem is all the living things in a place, together with their nonliving surroundings. The living parts are biotic factors. A deer eating acorns is biotic. The nonliving parts are abiotic factors. Sunlight, water, soil, and air are abiotic.

scenes.visual: ecosystem outline splits into green biotic side and yellow abiotic side

scenes.tts: Abiotic factors help decide which organisms can survive in a place. Few plants can grow on a forest floor that gets little sunlight. Water and floating mud block light. So few plants grow on the floor of deep or muddy water.

scenes.tts: Scientists often sort ecosystems into three broad groups. A terrestrial ecosystem is on land, like a forest. A freshwater ecosystem has water with very little salt, like a mountain stream. A marine ecosystem has salty ocean water. Salinity is the amount of salt dissolved in water.

scenes.visual: three panels with salt dots: none on land, few in stream, many in ocean

scenes.tts: Now follow the James downstream. An estuary is a place where fresh river water mixes with salty ocean water. The Chesapeake Bay is an estuary. Its salinity is in between, and it shifts with rain and season. As the river flows toward the Bay, salinity rises.

scenes.tts: Now think about the oysters. Eastern oysters can die when the water stays very low in salt for a long time. Brackish water is in between fresh and salty. Oyster reefs grow in the brackish lower James. The fresh water near Richmond is poor oyster habitat. So why do different living things live in different places? Abiotic factors such as salt and sunlight, together with the living things, decide who lives in each ecosystem.
